title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports Mathlib's factorization infrastructure (`Nat.Factorization.Basic`), the `Finsupp` type (used for factorizations as maps from primes to exponents), `Set.Finite` for infinite set statements, and `Filter.Basic` for eventual quantification. The `PrimeNormNum` import enables computational verification of primality for specific small numbers in the examples.
mathContext: The factorization $n = \prod p_i^{k_i}$ is represented as a `Finsupp \mathbb{N} \mathbb{N}$, mapping primes $p$ to their exponents $v_p(n)$. This is the key data structure enabling the injectivity condition.

title: Distinct Exponent Property
content: The predicate `HasDistinctExponents n` holds when the exponent map $p \mapsto v_p(n(n+1))$ is injective on the set of prime factors of $n(n+1)$. Here $v_p(m)$ denotes the $p$-adic valuation (exponent of $p$ in the factorization of $m$). Using Mathlib's `Nat.factorization` (a `Finsupp ℕ ℕ`) and `Set.InjOn`, this says no two distinct primes share the same exponent. The set $\{n : \text{HasDistinctExponents}(n)\}$ is called `DistinctExponentSet`.
mathContext: $\text{HasDistinctExponents}(n) \iff v_{p_1}(n(n+1)) \neq v_{p_2}(n(n+1))$ for all distinct primes $p_1, p_2 \mid n(n+1)$

title: Erdős Problem 913: Infinitude Conjecture
content: The central open question: Is $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : \text{HasDistinctExponents}(n)\}$ an infinite set? Since $\gcd(n, n+1) = 1$, the factorizations of $n$ and $n+1$ are disjoint, so the exponents of $n(n+1)$ are the union of exponents from $n$ and $n+1$ separately. The distinct-exponent condition requires that these two sets of exponents don't overlap and are individually injective. Formalized as `DistinctExponentSet.Infinite`.
mathContext: $|\{n : v_p(n(n+1)) \text{ injective on primes } p \mid n(n+1)\}| = \infty$?

title: The 8p²-1 Prime Pair Set
content: The set `PrimePairs8` $= \{p : p \text{ prime and } 8p^2 - 1 \text{ prime}\}$. Small examples: $p = 3$ gives $8 \cdot 9 - 1 = 71$ (prime); $p = 5$ gives $8 \cdot 25 - 1 = 199$ (prime); $p = 11$ gives $8 \cdot 121 - 1 = 967$ (prime). The infinitude of this set is a special case of the Bunyakovsky conjecture applied to $f(x) = 8x^2 - 1$, an irreducible polynomial with no fixed prime divisor. This is axiomatized since it is currently unproven.

title: Conditional Proof via 8p²-1 Construction
content: The key conditional result: if PrimePairs8 is infinite, then DistinctExponentSet is infinite. For each $p \in \text{PrimePairs8}$, set $n = 8p^2 - 1$. Then $n(n+1) = (8p^2 - 1) \cdot 8p^2 = (8p^2 - 1)^1 \cdot p^2 \cdot 2^3$. Since $8p^2 - 1$, $p$, and 2 are distinct primes (for $p \neq 2$), the exponents $\{1, 2, 3\}$ are all distinct. The map $p \mapsto 8p^2 - 1$ is injective on primes, so distinct $p$ values give distinct $n$ values, yielding infinitely many examples.

title: Small Examples
content: Concrete examples verifying the distinct exponent property: $n = 3$: $3 \cdot 4 = 2^2 \cdot 3^1$, exponents $\{2, 1\}$; $n = 7$: $7 \cdot 8 = 2^3 \cdot 7^1$, exponents $\{3, 1\}$; $n = 8$: $8 \cdot 9 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2$, exponents $\{3, 2\}$. Additional examples from the comment block: $n = 31$ ($31 \cdot 32 = 2^5 \cdot 31$, exponents $\{5, 1\}$) and $n = 127$ ($127 \cdot 128 = 2^7 \cdot 127$, exponents $\{7, 1\}$). The Mersenne-like pattern $n = 2^k - 1$ (when prime) always gives exponents $\{k, 1\}$.

title: Connection to Bunyakovsky Conjecture
content: The polynomial $f(x) = 8x^2 - 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}$ and has no fixed prime divisor (i.e., $\gcd(f(1), f(2), f(3), \ldots) = 1$). The Bunyakovsky conjecture (1857) predicts that such polynomials take infinitely many prime values. The Bateman-Horn conjecture (1962) even gives a conjectural density: the number of primes $p \leq N$ with $f(p)$ also prime should grow as $C \cdot N / (\log N)^2$ for an explicit constant $C$. Both conjectures remain open for all polynomials of degree $\geq 2$.
mathContext: Bunyakovsky conjecture: $f(x) = 8x^2 - 1$ irreducible, $\gcd_{n \geq 1} f(n) = 1 \implies |\{p \leq N : f(p) \text{ prime}\}| \to \infty$

title: Computing the Exponents {1, 2, 3}
content: The technical heart of the 8p²−1 path: `hasDistinctExponents_8p_sq` proves that for the three prime factors of $n(n+1)=(8p^2-1)(8p^2)$ the exponents are exactly $1$, $2$, $3$. Each valuation is computed separately by unfolding `factorization_mul` over the coprime split $n \cdot (n+1)$ and evaluating a `Finsupp.single`: $v_{8p^2-1}(m)=1$ (it divides $n$ once and not $n+1$, via `factorization_eq_zero_of_not_dvd` from coprimality), $v_p(m)=2$ (from $8p^2=2^3p^2$, using $p \nmid 8$), and $v_2(m)=3$ (from the $2^3$ in $8=2^3$, using $p \neq 2$). Coprimality of consecutive integers ($\gcd(n,n+1)=1$, via `coprime_self_add_right`) is what keeps the two factors' prime supports disjoint so the valuations don't mix.
mathContext: $v_{8p^2-1}(m)=1,\; v_p(m)=2,\; v_2(m)=3$ where $m=(8p^2-1)\cdot 2^3\cdot p^2$; disjointness from $\gcd(8p^2-1,\,8p^2)=1$

title: Assembling Infinitely Many Witnesses
content: `erdos_913_conditional` turns the pointwise construction into an infinitude statement. From the axiom that `PrimePairs8` is infinite, remove the single point $\{2\}$ (still infinite), map it injectively by $p \mapsto 8p^2-1$ (injectivity from `injective_8p_sq_minus_1`), so the image is infinite; then `Set.Infinite.mono` shows this image sits inside `DistinctExponentSet` because every such image point has distinct exponents by the valuation lemma. This is the standard 'inject an infinite set into the target' pattern: infinitude is inherited from the domain through an injection whose image lands in the desired set.

title: Concrete Witnesses (Two- and Three-Factor Cases)
content: The unconditional examples that make `DistinctExponentSet` provably nonempty right now, independent of any conjecture. `hasDistinctExponents_of_primeFactors_pair` is the two-prime analogue of the triple helper, reducing the `InjOn` condition to a single inequality of exponents. The witnesses $n \in \{3,7,8,31,127\}$ are the pair case (two prime factors, e.g. $127\cdot 128 = 2^7\cdot 127^1$), while $n=71$ is the three-factor case $71\cdot 72 = 2^3\cdot 3^2\cdot 71$ — exactly the $p=3$ instance of the $8p^2-1$ construction ($8\cdot 9-1=71$). Each is discharged by `native_decide` on the concrete product, which is why the file's axiom profile includes `Lean.ofReduceBool`.

title: Naming the Governing Hypothesis
content: `Bunyakovsky8 := PrimePairs8.Infinite` gives the open hypothesis a name that records its provenance: it is the Bunyakovsky/Bateman–Horn conjecture specialized to $f(x)=8x^2-1$. Packaging the assumption as a named `Prop` (rather than only as the `axiom`) documents that the $8p^2-1$ conditional is *exactly as hard as* this instance of a famous conjecture — the entry is honest that Erdős #913 is here reduced to, not resolved by, an unproven statement.

title: An Independent Mersenne Route
content: A second, logically independent sufficient condition. For a Mersenne prime $2^k-1$ (with $k\ge 2$), take $n = 2^k-1$; then $n(n+1) = (2^k-1)\cdot 2^k$ has just two prime factors with exponents $\{1, k\}$, automatically distinct since $k \ge 2$. `hasDistinctExponents_mersenne` computes these valuations and `erdos_913_conditional_mersenne` again lifts to infinitude via an injective image (`injective_mersenne`: $k \mapsto 2^k-1$). Thus **infinitely many Mersenne primes** would also settle Erdős #913 — a well-known open conjecture distinct from the $8p^2-1$ hypothesis. The file closes with `nonempty_distinctExponentSet`, recording that the set is unconditionally nonempty (witnessed by $n=3$).
